newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Interior minister escapes Russian cabinet shakeup.
newsitem.headline: Interior minister escapes Russian cabinet shakeup.

text.p: Conservative Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov was left untouched in President Boris Yeltsin's cabinet shake-up on Monday, making him one of the great survivors in the Russian government.

His ministry has become the most prominent of the three organisations collectively known as Russia's "power ministries", an indication of their strategic importance in a country still prone to political instability.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's announcement gave no word on the fate of the leaders of the other two -- Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and Nikolai Kovalyov, head of the Federal Security Service which succeeded the KGB.
Rodionov came under fire from Yeltsin last month but held an hour-long meeting with him on Monday and analysts say he is likely to retain his post, at least for now.
Kovaylov's name has not come up in the media speculation surrounding the reorganisation, said to have involved furious behind-the-scenes bargaining.
The reshuffle, expected to be completed later in the week, was aimed at tackling not just an economic slide but also the burgeoning corruption which has left the public disenchanted with reform.
Yeltsin called last month for a revamped cabinet, saying he was dissatisfied with the government's failure to tackle Russia's deep-seated economic and social problems.
But while he also acknowledged that the government was loosing the fight against crime, far from firing Kulikov, he promoted him to the higher rank of deputy prime minister and widened his brief.

The new line-up involved sweeping changes bringing in younger, reform-minded people. The 50-year-old career Interior Ministry soldier, already considered the cabinet's most conservative member, thus stood out even more.
He was an advocate of the use of force to smash separatist rebels in Chechnya which Yeltsin has since admitted was one of the biggest mistakes of his presidency.
But Kulikov, appointed in 1995 and put in charge last month of the tax police, customs service and other agencies dealing with economic crime, is above all loyal to the president.
"Yeltsin has really done what he was expected to do in this case," said Sergei Markov, an analyst with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think tank.

He said Kulikov was popular with the police, making him a valuable asset for Yeltsin, especially in view of a planned nationwide strike on March 27 which some opposition figures say could lead to widespread unrest.
Yeltsin rapped Rodionov, who took over the defence portfolio last July, for publicly "whining" about the problems facing Russia's demoralised, cash-strapped armed forces.

Rodionov subseqently cancelled planned trips to Armenia and Georgia and a visit to an international arms exhibition in the United Arab Emirates on March 16-20, fuelling speculation that he might lose his job.

But he seemed to mend fences with Yeltsin on Monday, rowing back on comments last month in which he expressed concern that underfunding of the armed forces raised doubts about the reliabilty of Russia's nuclear weapons.
The Kremlin said he had assured Yeltsin that the command and control system governing Russia's nuclear missiles was reliable.
Rodionov, 60, says he supports Yeltsin's plans to reform the military but has called for extra cash to finance the reforms.
"There is no information but I think he will stay. It is what the army as a whole wants," Markov said.
Andrei Kortunov from the Russian Science Foundation was less sure. "There are some key nominations to come," he said. "We have to wait and see if Rodionov stays or who might replace him."
